F1.quote: "Sappho 31 is a lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of the island of Lesbos."
F1.claim: A lyric poem by the Archaic Greek poet Sappho of Lesbos

F2.quote: "The poem is also known as phainetai moi (φαίνεταί μοι lit. 'It seems to me') after the opening words of its first line"
F2.claim: Also known as phainetai moi, from its opening words

F3.quote: "as the Ode to Anactoria, based on a conjecture that its subject is Anactoria, a woman mentioned elsewhere by Sappho"
F3.claim: The title Ode to Anactoria rests on a conjecture

F4.quote: "It is one of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman."
F4.claim: One of Sappho's most famous poems, describing her love for a young woman

F5.quote: "preserved in the first-century AD treatise on aesthetics On the Sublime"
F5.claim: Preserved in the first-century AD treatise On the Sublime

F6.quote: "Four stanzas are well-preserved, followed by part of one more line; this, as well as Catullus' adaptation of the poem, suggests that there was originally one more stanza of the poem,"
F6.claim: Four stanzas and part of a line survive; probably one more stanza originally

F7.quote: "A reconstruction of the poem by classicist Armand D'Angour suggests that the original poem may have had up to 8 stanzas."

F8.quote: "Fragment 31 is composed in Sapphic stanzas, a metrical form named after Sappho and consisting of stanzas of three long followed by one short line."

F9.quote: "The poem is written in the Aeolic dialect"

F10.quote: "The poem centres around three characters: a man and a woman, both otherwise unidentified, and the speaker."
F10.claim: Three characters: a man, a woman, the speaker

F11.quote: "The context of the poem has been the subject of much scholarly debate: Thomas McEvilley calls it the "central controversy" about the poem."
F11.claim: The poem's context is debated; McEvilley's 'central controversy'

F12.quote: "Wilamowitz suggested that the poem was a wedding song, and that the man mentioned in the initial stanza of the poem was the bridegroom."
F12.claim: Wilamowitz: a wedding song, the man the bridegroom

F13.quote: "Since the second half of the twentieth century, scholars have tended to follow Denys Page in dismissing the wedding-song argument."
F13.claim: Scholars since mid-century follow Page in dismissing the wedding-song argument

F14.quote: "the man's role is to act as a "contrast figure","

F15.quote: "John Winkler argues that "'That man' in poem 31 is like the military armament in poem 16, an introductory set-up to be dismissed"."
F15.claim: Winkler: that man is an introductory set-up to be dismissed

F16.quote: "As far back as the eighteenth century, it has been proposed that the poem is about Sappho's jealousy of the man who sits with her beloved."
F16.claim: Since the eighteenth century the poem has been read as jealousy

F17.quote: "Though this is still a popular interpretation of the poem, many critics deny that the fragment is about jealousy at all."
F17.claim: Many critics deny the poem is about jealousy

F18.quote: "Anne Carson argues that Sappho has no wish to take the man's place, nor is she concerned that he will usurp hers: thus, she is not jealous of him, but amazed at his ability to retain his composure so close to the object of her desire."
F18.claim: Carson: not jealousy, amazement at his composure

F19.quote: "Joan DeJean criticises the "jealousy" interpretation of the poem as intended to play down the homoeroticism of the poem."
F19.claim: DeJean: the jealousy reading plays down the homoeroticism

F20.quote: "Armand D'Angour argues that the phrase ἀλλὰ πὰν τόλματον means "all must be dared", rather than "endured" as it is sometimes translated."

F21.quote: "An alternative reading is suggested by Gallavotti: according to his thesis, the text was corrupted over time as a result of the disappearance of the sound [w]"
F21.claim: Gallavotti: the opening corrupted by loss of digamma (phainetai woi)

F22.quote: "In 1970, an article by Hungarian-French psychoanalyst George Devereux suggested that what Sappho is describing here is a seizure, pointing that the symptoms listed in the fragment are the same symptoms of an anxiety attack."
F22.claim: Devereux (1970): the symptoms are those of an anxiety attack

F23.quote: "according to Emmet Robbins, "probably the single most famous poem to come down from Antiquity"."
F23.claim: Robbins: probably the most famous poem from Antiquity

F24.quote: "has been the subject of more scholarly commentary than any other of her works."
F24.claim: More commentary than any other of Sappho's works

F25.quote: "In ancient Rome, the poet Catullus adapted it into his 51st poem, putting his muse Lesbia into the role of Sappho's beloved."
F25.claim: Catullus adapted it as poem 51, with Lesbia as the beloved

F26.quote: "The ancient Greek authors Theocritus and Apollonius of Rhodes both adapted the poem"

F27.quote: "The poem is quoted in Longinus's treatise On the Sublime for the intensity of its emotion,"
F27.claim: Longinus quotes it for the intensity of its emotion

F28.quote: "Plato draws on it in Socrates' second speech on love in the Phaedrus,"
F28.claim: Plato draws on it in the Phaedrus

F29.quote: "In the nineteenth century, the poem began to be seen as an exemplar of Romantic lyric,"
F29.claim: Nineteenth century: an exemplar of Romantic lyric

F30.quote: "This deservedly famous poem is quoted in the first- or third-century A.D. treatise On the Sublime attributed to Longinus"
F30.claim: Quoted in On the Sublime, first- or third-century, attributed to Longinus

F31.quote: "the selection of the most striking of them and their combination into a single whole that has produced the singular excellence of the passage"
F31.claim: Longinus: excellence lies in selecting and combining the symptoms

F32.quote: "scholars have spent a lot of time trying to pinpoint the significance of the man in the first stanza, and whether Sappho’s symptoms are of eros or envy."
F32.claim: Scholars debate the man and whether the symptoms are eros or envy

F33.quote: "that very “unpin-down-able” quality, that slippery multivalence under a limpid surface, the strangeness at the heart, is an intimate part of the poem’s appeal."
F33.claim: Childers: the poem's multivalence is part of its appeal

F34.quote: "Though it feels complete, the poem is a fragment: for some reason “Longinus” leaves off his quotation one line into the fifth stanza, which begins “Still, all must be endured, since even a poor…”"
F34.claim: The quotation breaks off one line into the fifth stanza

F35.quote: "Catullus goes a different way in the final stanza of his famous free translation, poem 51"
F35.claim: Catullus 51, a free translation, diverges in its final stanza

F36.quote: "Today’s lyric poem was written in the fifth century B.C., although it reads as if it were written yesterday."
F36.claim: Jackson dates the poem to the fifth century B.C.

F37.quote: "The portrait of a speaker viscerally filled with jealousy is evidence of the endurance of human emotions across the ages."
F37.claim: Jackson: a speaker filled with jealousy; emotions endure

F38.quote: "The poem describes the response of the speaker, a woman, to watching another woman talking to a man. (The grammar of the original Greek makes the gender of each figure clear.)"
F38.claim: The speaker is a woman watching another woman talking to a man; the Greek makes genders clear

F39.quote: "then, in an extraordinary switch, focuses in detail on herself and her own intense contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire."
F39.claim: The poem switches to the speaker's contradictory bodily emotions of jealousy and desire

F40.quote: "as preserved (through a quotation in On the Sublime, a Roman Imperial–era Greek treatise), it seems to be missing the ending."
F40.claim: Preserved by quotation in On the Sublime; seems to lack its ending

F41.quote: "The fragmentary final stanza is treated differently by the translators: Barnard skips it altogether; Carson treats it as a call to action, and Poochigian presents it as a moment of self-hating submission."
F41.claim: Translators treat the fragmentary final stanza differently

F42.quote: "Catullus, who had access to the whole original, provides a very different final stanza."
F42.claim: Catullus had the whole original and wrote a very different final stanza

F43.quote: "this is unambiguously a poem about same-sex desire."
F43.claim: Unambiguously a poem about same-sex desire

F44.quote: "In the original, Sappho uses a series of different syntactical subjects for the sentence that straddles the third and fourth stanzas: “tongue,” “fire,” “seeing/eyes,” “hearing/ears,” “sweat,” and “trembling” are all grammatical subjects of the verbs—rather than “I.”"
F44.claim: The body parts, not 'I', are the grammatical subjects; Carson keeps this

F45.quote: "The theory that Sappho’s emotions are that of jealousy and envy is a major theory put forward by many critics."
F45.claim: The jealousy theory is a major theory among critics

F46.quote: "The identification of ‘that man’ in Sappho’s best-known poem, has proven to be one of the most complex and difficult problems in the interpretation of her extant poetry."
F46.claim: Identifying 'that man' is among the hardest problems

F47.quote: "Longinus, a Greek teacher writing under the Roman Empire hundreds of years after Sappho’s lifetime, explains what is so unforgettable about Sappho"
F47.claim: Longinus, writing under the Roman Empire, explains its excellence

F48.quote: "This poem has no explicit mention of a marriage"
F48.claim: The poem does not mention marriage
